mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

head: Tool

blocks.text: Lay your 7 tool cards in a row. Which tool have you used before?

slides.note: The toolbox page for the tools we have met in the term, one use for each (taught again for anyone who joins cold). Read each row aloud. Children lay the 7 tool cards in a row and point to one they have used. Say: today we do not learn a new tool; we practise choosing one. A child with no cards writes the 7 names on small papers. Children answer aloud. No writing.

slides.title: Draw it: two strips

blocks.text: Ali has 9 sweets. Mei has 5 sweets. How many more sweets does Ali have?

slides.note: Draw it, used on a tiny problem (Term 2 Lesson 2, taught again). The gap between the two strips is how many more: 9 take away 5 is 4. Children answer aloud: 4. A child who is unsure counts the extra squares on the long strip.

slides.title: Work backwards: go back

blocks.text: I think of a number. I add 4. I get 11. What is my number?

slides.note: Work backwards, used on a tiny problem. Start at the end, 11, and go back 4: 7. Check forwards: 7 and 4 make 11. Children answer aloud: 7. A child who is unsure counts back 4 on fingers from 11.

slides.title: Spot the pattern

blocks.text: 3, 6, 9, ... What comes next? What do we add each time?

slides.note: Spot the pattern, used on a tiny problem. Each number is 3 more than the one before, so the next number is 12. Children answer aloud: 12 and add 3. A child who is unsure counts on 3 from 9 on fingers. No writing.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Your paper is not collected.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Today is Monday.
What day is it 3 days later?

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: A number add 6 is 15.
What is the number?
I know because ___.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 is an access question; puzzle 2 is a thinking question. Neither says which tool to use. Puzzle 1: 3 days later than Monday is Thursday (count on from tomorrow). Puzzle 2: 15 take away 6 is 9. A child who adds 15 and 6 gets 21: say nothing yet. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; your paper is not collected. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper to the camera. There is no private chat. Do not reveal answers until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list.

rows: A film starts at 3:30 and lasts 1 hour. When does it end?

Row 1 has 2 stars, row 2 has 4 stars, row 3 has 6 stars. How many stars are in row 8?

Card 1 fits Draw it (a number line) or Act it out (a clock). Card 2 fits List every way, or Guess and check. Card 3 fits Make a table or Spot the pattern. blocks.text: Did the words tell us the tool? Not always. We looked at the problem.

slides.note: Show after the children have chosen. Say: the words did not tell us the tool, we looked at the problem. Praise a reason, never speed.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: Did one word tell us the tool?
Can two tools fit the same problem?
What can we do if a tool is too slow?

slides.note: About 2 minutes. Ask each question and take volunteers. Listen for: no single word gives the tool; two tools can fit; a different tool can be quicker. Do not give the rule first. Say: in the Mini-lesson we solve one problem with two tools, and then one where the first tool is too slow.

slides.title: Tool 1: draw it

blocks.text: Kumar has $15. He buys a cup for $6 and a rubber for $4. How much money is left?

slides.note: One problem, two tools. Tool 1: Draw it. One long strip of 15, mark off 6, then 4. What is left is the last part. Children draw their own strip on paper while you wait 10 seconds. Answer on the next slide.

slides.title: Draw it: $5 left

blocks.text: 6 and 4 are spent. 5 is left. Kumar has $5 left.

slides.note: The strip shows 6, then 4, and 5 left. Say: draw it works well when we can see the parts.

slides.title: Tool 2: work backwards

blocks.text: Same problem. Start at 15. Take away 6. Then take away 4.

slides.note: Tool 2: Work backwards (here it is just taking away, step by step, from what Kumar had). Children say 15 take away 6 is 9, then 9 take away 4 is 5. Answer on the next slide.

slides.title: Both tools say $5

blocks.text: Both tools say 5. Check a third way: 6 + 4 + 5 = 15.

slides.note: Both tools give 5. Ask: which tool was quicker for you? Take two answers; both are fine. Then show the check a third way: spent 6 and 4, left 5; 6 and 4 make 10, and 10 and 5 make 15, which is what Kumar had. Say: when two tools agree and the check works, we can trust the answer.

slides.title: The first tool is too slow

blocks.text: 1 square with a handle uses 5 sticks. 2 squares use 8 sticks. 3 squares use 11 sticks. How many sticks do 8 squares use?

slides.note: A problem where the first tool gets stuck. Say: try draw it. Children start to draw 8 squares with sticks on paper. After about a minute stop them: it is slow, we may slip, and the picture is huge. Say: Wait. Try a tool. Ask: which tool could be quicker? Take volunteers (a table or a pattern). Do not say the answer yet.

slides.title: Make a table: 26 sticks

blocks.text: Each square adds 3 sticks. 8 squares use 26 sticks.

slides.note: The table: 5, 8, 11, then add 3 each time: 14, 17, 20, 23, 26. Check another way: the first square and its handle use 5, and 7 more squares each add 3 sticks: 5 and 21 make 26. Say: when a tool is too slow, we change tool. We did not do anything wrong: drawing was a good start.

slides.title: When we are stuck

items: Wait.
Try a tool.
Try a smaller case.
Ask.

blocks.text: Say it with me.

slides.note: The stuck routine, in the same words as the Toolbox Card: Wait. Try a tool. Try a smaller case. Ask. Say it with the children twice. A smaller case means smaller numbers, for example 2 squares first. A child who is still stuck may tick I am still stuck on the look-back page.

slides.title: Mime the tools

blocks.text: Stand up. Mime each tool with me.
Draw a long strip in the air. Count on your fingers. Tap a table.
Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera with a little clear space. Mime each tool slowly: draw a long strip in the air (Draw it); walk on the spot with counters in your hands (Act it out); clap a steady beat that gets louder each time (Spot the pattern); write a list in the air (List every way); tap a table (Make a table); walk backwards two steps (Work backwards); point, then thumbs up or thumbs down (Guess and check). No equipment, no running. A child may stay seated and tap the desk softly. Do not give prizes or compare children. investigation.answer: Many answers are right. A good problem names a thing to find, has numbers that fit the tool, and has one answer. For example, for Work backwards: Mei had some sweets. She ate 4 and has 7 left. How many sweets did Mei have? Answer: 11.

challenge_quest.title: Mi's Challenge Quest
challenge_quest.where: Term 3 Lesson 10 (the last lesson of the term), minutes 35 to 55, the part Mi's Challenge Quest, straight after the brain break; or at the make-up slot
challenge_quest.plan_note: The end-of-term slot is a game with Mi, not a test. The group plays it in pairs (a child and a quest partner) or as a group quest with Mi, on private paper. No score or mark is shown to the child, there is no ranking and no visible timer. The tutor keeps private notes only, for one line to each grown-up and for advice for next term's group. It keeps the 20-minute slot after the break: 8 short gates and one optional secret cave item, all at Start here level. Six gates visit the lessons of the term (Term 3 Lessons 1 to 3 share gate 1, Term 3 Lessons 5 and 6 share gate 3); gates 7 and 8 are mixed gates with no lesson tag. Under each gate the child circles the tool they used and ticks I checked: the quest is where the child chooses the tool, so no gate names one. Gate 6 asks the child to check a sum a friend wrote. The secret cave joins two ideas the group has met (money and listing) in an unseen way and asks why the child chose a tool. A middle child needs about 17 minutes of reading aloud and quiet work; a slower child may use a few minutes of the workbook time to finish. The Quest Log carries the Term 3 pictures (a clock, coins, price tags, a calendar and a stick pattern). Time is written as digits with am or pm; money with the cent sign.
challenge_quest.story: Mi the dolphin is swimming to the Pearl Cave. Eight gates are in the way, and each gate has one puzzle. At the end there is an optional secret cave.
child_rules: Mi needs your help at 8 gates. Talk with your quest partner, then write your own answer.
It is not a race. Your answers are private. You may skip a gate: Mi swims round it.
challenge_quest.child_footer: Math Inquirers Term 3 Mi's Challenge Quest.
page_instructions: Gates 1 and 2: Mi needs your help. Write your answers in the spaces.
Gates 5 and 6: nearly there. Circle Yes or No where you see it.
Gates 7 and 8, and the secret cave: the last stretch.

questions.say: Gate 1. Look at the clock. Part a: the time is blank. Part b: breakfast is at 7:00. Write am or pm. Part c: a film starts at 2:30. It lasts half an hour. It ends at blank.
questions.solution: The long hand is on the 7, which is 35 minutes. The short hand is just before the 5, so the hour is 4: 4:35. Breakfast is in the morning: am. Half an hour after half past 2 is 3 o'clock.
mistakes: (a) 7:20 or 5:35 (the two hands read the wrong way round).

questions.say: Gate 2. Look at the coins. Part a: the coins make blank cents. Part b: Mei pays 10 dollars for a toy that costs 7 dollars. Her change is blank dollars.
questions.solution: 50 and 20 make 70, and 20 more is 90, and 5 more is 95 cents. Count up from 7 to 10: 3 dollars change.

questions.solution: 9 is more than 6, so the ruler costs more. Count up from 6 to 9: $3 more. 4 and 6 make 10, and 5 and 5 would need two $5 tags.
questions.right: All correct (the two prices in either order).

parts.text: A week after the 3rd is the ___ th.

questions.solution: Saturday is 1, Sunday is 2, Monday is 3. A week is 7 days: 3 and 7 make 10.

questions.text: 1 triangle with a handle uses 4 sticks. 2 triangles use 6 sticks. The picture shows 3 triangles: 8 sticks.
questions.say: Gate 5. 1 triangle with a handle uses 4 sticks. 2 triangles use 6 sticks. The picture shows 3 triangles: 8 sticks. Part a: 4 triangles use blank sticks. Part b: 5 triangles use blank sticks.
questions.solution: Each new triangle adds 2 sticks: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. A row of 4 triangles uses 10 sticks and a row of 5 triangles uses 12 sticks.

questions.skill: Check a sum a friend wrote (Term 3 Lesson 9)
questions.text: A child in another class writes 49 + 38 = 77.

parts.text: Is the answer right? Circle Yes or No. [yesno]

questions.say: Gate 6. A child in another class writes 49 plus 38 equals 77. Part a: is the answer right? Circle Yes or No. Part b: the right answer is blank.
questions.solution: 77 take away 38 is 39, not 49, so 77 is wrong. 9 and 8 make 17: 1 ten and 7 ones, so 40 and 30 and 10 and 7 make 87.

questions.skill: Money left over, and how much there was at first (mixed: no lesson tag)
questions.text: Mei buys a toy for $6. Now she has $9 left.
questions.say: Gate 7. Mei buys a toy for 6 dollars. Now she has 9 dollars left. Mei had blank dollars at first.
questions.solution: She spent 6 and has 9 left, so she had 9 and 6, which is 15. Check: 15 take away 6 is 9.

questions.skill: Four coins that make an amount (mixed: no lesson tag)
questions.text: Ben has 4 coins. They are 5-cent coins and 10-cent coins. They make 25 cents.

parts.text: Ben has ___ five-cent coins and ___ ten-cent coins.

questions.say: Gate 8. Ben has 4 coins. They are 5-cent coins and 10-cent coins. They make 25 cents. Write how many five-cent coins and how many ten-cent coins.
questions.solution: Try 2 and 2: 10 and 20 make 30, too high. Try 3 and 1: 15 and 10 make 25. That is 4 coins.

optional.skill: Exactly $14 with $2 notes and $5 notes (money and listing joined)
optional.text: Think harder (optional). Ali has lots of $2 notes and $5 notes. He pays exactly $14.

parts.text: One way: ___ two-dollar notes and ___ five-dollar notes.
Is there another way? Circle Yes or No. [yesno]

optional.say: The secret cave has one more puzzle, and it is optional. You may skip it. Ali has lots of 2-dollar notes and 5-dollar notes. He pays exactly 14 dollars. Part a: write one way. Part b: is there another way? Circle Yes or No.
optional.answer: Seven $2 notes, or two $2 notes and two $5 notes; yes, there are 2 ways
optional.solution: Seven $2 notes make 14. Two $5 notes make 10, and 2 two-dollar notes make 4, so 10 and 4 make 14. One $5 note leaves 9 and three $5 notes make 15, which do not work, so there are exactly 2 ways.
mistakes: A way that does not add to 14.
Saying there is only one way.
optional.note: Never marked and never counted. Whether the child tried it adds one neutral phrase to the line for the grown-up; a skipped cave adds nothing.

give: A week before: send the grown-up note (L30_Quest_Parent_Note.pdf). The Quest Log (4 pages) is in each child's Term 3 book: families keep it closed in an envelope and find a quest partner (a grown-up or a brother or sister). A family whose book has a missing or damaged Quest Log page tells you: arrange another way (for example the make-up slot, with L30_Quest_Log.pdf sent to the family another way).

Tell the group in the opening and at slide s-quest1: this is Mi's Challenge Quest, a game with Mi. Everyone works on their own paper with a quest partner beside them. It is not a race, a gate may be skipped, and nothing is shown to the group.

Start at minute 35 (straight after the brain break) and finish by minute 55. Children open the Quest Log only when you say. The paper lies flat on the table and is never held up. The quest partner may talk about how to start and ask 'how do you know?', but does not give answers. Cameras may be on or off. Use your own watch out of sight of the camera: no clock, countdown or timer is ever shown to the children.

Read each page aloud, one gate at a time (the script has the words), then leave quiet working time: about 2.5 minutes for page 1, 3 for page 2, 3 for page 3 and 3 for page 4. After each page say that the gates are open and Mi swims on, whatever the answers. Say nothing about right or wrong, and read no answers. A middle child needs about 17 minutes in all; a slower child may finish in the first minutes of the workbook.

Allowed: fingers, counters and talk with the quest partner. Not allowed: a calculator, a grown-up giving answers, looking at the workbook. A child who finishes early turns the Quest Log over and draws quietly.

After page 2, take a one-minute stretch (stand, shake out, sip water). After page 4, show slide s-quest2. Do not collect or look at any Quest Log. While children work, notice (do not write on the shared screen) how they start: counters, a clock face, coins, drawing, talking to the partner.
after: Same day: the grown-up takes ONE clear photo of each of the 4 pages (page flat, taken straight from above, the whole page in view, and the name on each page) and sends them to the program's business WhatsApp, +65 9880 5962, and to no other number. Never to a child, never to a personal phone, never into the class chat.

Within 3 days: open the photos only on the business WhatsApp (never on a personal phone) and write your private notes (section 5) for each child, from the photos and what you saw on camera. Section 4 shows what each answer tells you. Nothing is written on the child's paper, nothing is added up and no order of children is made. Nothing about the quest goes back to the child or the group except thanks.

Write ONE line for each grown-up from your notes (section 7): what we saw, in plain words, and one small next step if it helps. It is sent to the parent only. No marks, no x out of 8, no ranking, no comparison with other children, no prediction.

Fill in the group advice sheet (section 6): what several children were still working on, with no names, and what you will do in the first lessons of next term. It is kept for next term's tutor and is never shown to families.

Once the line is sent, save the photos to the program's private file store and delete them from the business WhatsApp chat. The program keeps the photos for 90 days after the program ends, then deletes them, as the privacy notice says. Delete each child's notes sheet when the line is sent (keep only the line in the family file, and the group advice sheet). Never forward the photos or save them to a personal phone or any other device.
At the start of next term say to the whole group: thank you for playing Mi's Challenge Quest; there is nothing to share and nothing to fear. Never name a child or an answer.
late: A child who was away or whose family prefers another time: plays the quest at the make-up slot BEFORE watching the recording (the quest is not on the recording, so no gate is given away). It is a small group or a pair with Mi, with a parent beside the child on camera. The tutor never sits alone with one child on a private call.

A child who joined late: the family may choose to leave out gates for lessons the child did not attend. Write nothing for those gates; if no gate of an area was taught, the line for the grown-up says nothing about that area.
A family that does not want the quest: no problem. The child does the Term 3 Lesson 10 work as usual and the line for the grown-up uses your own notes from the lessons only.
A child who is upset or stuck: remind the group (open session) that every gate can be skipped and Mi swims round it. Do not single the child out. The grown-up may stop the quest at any time.

A family whose Quest Log is missing or damaged: tell the family to say so a week before and arrange another way (for example the make-up slot, with L30_Quest_Log.pdf sent to the family another way). Never ask a child about it in front of the group.
privacy_checklist: Quest Logs are never held up to the camera and never read out.
No answer is said aloud during or after the quest. Gates open for everyone, whatever the answers.
No clock, countdown or timer is shown; nobody is told who finished first or last.

Photos come to the program's business WhatsApp (+65 9880 5962) only; tutors never use a personal phone; photos are kept 90 days after the program ends, then deleted; the line goes to the parent only; no private message to any child.

No score, no x out of 8, no ranking, no comparison between children, and no tally or count of any kind on a child's page or anywhere a family can see. In your own notes: words only. You may circle one of the three words (with help / with a prompt / on their own) for each habit in the private notes sheet (section 5); never add the circles up, never compare children, and never say or show the words to a child or a grown-up.

The recording captures the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted: the recording is paused for the whole quest (slides s-quest1 and s-quest2) and restarted for the workbook. The WhatsApp number is never on a slide.

lines.text: @rec
Greet each child by first name as they arrive. Then start the recording.

Hello, inquirers! Please stay muted unless I invite you to speak. Cameras on if you can, so I can see you; cameras off is fine too. Pencil ready, and your tool cards and your closed Quest Log on the table.

Now one problem with two tools. Kumar has fifteen dollars. He buys a cup for six dollars and a rubber for four dollars. How much money is left?
Tool one: draw it. Draw one long strip for fifteen. Mark off six, then four.
Children draw a strip on their own paper.
Six and four are spent. Five is left. Kumar has five dollars left.
Tool two: work backwards. Start at fifteen. Take away six. Then take away four.
Children say the two steps.
Fifteen take away six is nine. Nine take away four is five. Both tools say five dollars.
Which tool was quicker for you?
Check a third way. Six and four and five make fifteen. When two tools agree and the check works, we can trust the answer.
A new problem. Squares in a row with a handle, made of sticks. One square uses five sticks, two squares use eight, three squares use eleven. How many sticks do eight squares use? Try draw it.
Children start to draw eight squares. Stop them after about a minute.
Wait. Drawing eight squares takes too long, and we might slip. Try another tool.
Which tool could be quicker?
Make a table. Five, eight, eleven. Each square adds three sticks: fourteen, seventeen, twenty, twenty-three, twenty-six. Eight squares use twenty-six sticks.
How can we check twenty-six another way?

talk.question: A pattern has 20 pictures. Each one has 3 more sticks. One child in another class says: I will draw all 20 pictures. Another child says: I will make a table. Which tool would you pick first? Why?
talk.answer: Both tools can work. A table is quicker for the 20th picture, because we add 3 each time and drawing 20 pictures is slow. Spotting the pattern also works: 4 and 19 lots of 3.
talk.look_for: A tool named with a reason, not just a name. Credit any reason about speed, slips or being able to see it.

menu.title: Can two tools agree?
menu.tutor: A child says: two different tools can give the same answer. Is that always true? Try it with: a number add 8 is 17.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Solve a number add 8 is 17 with two tools. Do both tools agree?
menu.answer: Yes, if both are used well. Work backwards: 17 take away 8 is 9. Guess and check: try 9, and 9 and 8 make 17.
